title: Matter
hook: twenty-eight kinds of matter, beginning with the four great elements

segments.voice: Yesterday, compassion and wisdom: not traits a person owns, but factors that arise in a moment and pass. Your line: compassion is a moment.

Press a fingertip against the table, or your knee, or the arm of the chair. Something pushes back. It's hard, or soft. It's warm, or cool. Leave it there a moment and there's a faint press, a little give, maybe the beat of a pulse. For days this path has looked at the mind, factor by factor. Today the Abhidhamma turns to the other side of its world: the stuff that pushes back. It has one word for all of it, and it begins its list with four.
screen: `PRESS A FINGERTIP DOWN.` → `SOMETHING PUSHES BACK.` → `THE OTHER SIDE OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: You met these four in the body back on day two hundred fifty-four. Today they get a closer look. The word is rupa: form, or matter. In one sutta the Buddha plays on a verb that means to be afflicted. It's called rupa, he says, because it gets afflicted: by cold and heat, hunger and thirst, flies and mosquitoes, wind and sun. Matter, in this telling, is the part of you that can be bitten. The manual called the Abhidhammattha Sangaha counts twenty-eight kinds of matter, and it begins with four great elements: earth, water, fire and air. These aren't soil, rain, flame and wind. They're qualities. Earth is hardness and softness, what pushes back. Water is cohesion, what holds a thing together and lets it flow. Fire is heat, and cold too. Air is motion and support, the way air keeps a tire firm. Every bit of matter, the manual says, has all four, in different measure. A stone is mostly earth, yet it still holds together, has a temperature, presses. And a strange detail: in this system, water can't be touched. Put a hand in a stream, and touch meets softness, coolness and pressure: earth, fire and air. Cohesion is known by the mind, not the skin. The old suttas use the same four to look at the body: hair and bones as earth, blood and sweat as water, warmth as fire, breath as air. And of each one they say: this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
screen: `RUPA: WHAT CAN BE BITTEN.` · `FOUR ELEMENTS ARE FOUR QUALITIES.` · `WATER CAN'T BE TOUCHED.` · then, large: `NOT MINE, NOT ME, NOT MY SELF.`

segments.voice: Feel the four, one at a time: earth in the weight of you on the seat, then water, the mind's sense of your body holding together as one shape. Then fire, warmth in your hands and coolness at the tip of the nose, and air, the breath pressing the chest out and letting it settle back. If attention drifts, begin again at earth.
Rupa. Form, matter: the part of the world that can be pressed, warmed, moved and bitten, beginning with four great elements. Today's word.
Your line: four great elements. Hardness, cohesion, heat and motion, in every bit of matter, your own hand included. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Abhidhamma study, students learn the four great elements as qualities of matter, and in meditation some Theravada traditions teach attending to earth, water, fire and air in the body one by one.

chat.meaning: The four great elements are qualities found in every bit of matter, not soil, rain, flame and wind: earth is hardness, water cohesion, fire heat, air motion.

rupa.meaning: form, matter: what can be pressed, warmed, moved and bitten

notes: Twenty-eight kinds of matter: stated from Abhidhammattha Sangaha VI; confirm.
SN 22.79: the Buddha's wordplay on ruppati (afflicted, 'deformed') and the list cold, heat, hunger, thirst, flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun (creeping things omitted). Paraphrased; confirm.
'Water can't be touched': the tangible object (photthabba) is earth, fire and air in the Dhammasangani and later manuals; cohesion known by mind-door. Confirm phrasing.
MN 28 lists for each element (hair, bones; blood, sweat; warmth; breath) and the refrain 'this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self' are paraphrased, not quoted; confirm.
The tire simile for the air element (distension/support) is the writer's own image.
